n: Woe to Ariel — a poetic name for Jerusalem, David’s city. Its people go through their yearly festivals and sacrifices, but mere routine won’t save them. Nephi applies much of this chapter to the last days in 2 Nephi 26–27.

f.g: Possibly “lion of God” or “altar hearth” — the place where sacrifices burn.

n: God will bring distress on Ariel, with mourning and grief; the city will become like an altar hearth — a place of burning.

f.w: it shall be unto me as Ariel
f.g: A wordplay: the city will become like an “altar hearth” of slaughter.

n: God Himself will encircle Jerusalem with siege camps, towers, and ramps — through Assyria and later Babylon.

Brought low, Jerusalem will speak from the ground, its voice whispering from the dust like a ghost. Nephi applies this to his own people, whose record would speak “out of the dust” — the Book of Mormon.

f.w: thy speech shall whisper out of the dust

f.g: Here a faint, low voice, like that of the dead.

n: But suddenly the hordes of enemies will become like fine dust and blowing chaff — in an instant.
The Lord of hosts will come with thunder, earthquake, a great noise, storm, and devouring fire. Nephi applies this to the destruction among his people before Christ’s visit.
All the nations that attack Ariel and its stronghold will vanish like a dream in the night.
They will be like a hungry man who dreams of eating and wakes up still hungry, or a thirsty man who dreams of drinking and wakes up parched. Their conquest will never satisfy.

f.w: all the nations be, that fight against mount Zion

n: Be astonished and blinded! The people stagger as if drunk — not from wine, but from spiritual stupor.
The Lord has poured over them a spirit of deep sleep, closing the eyes of prophets and covering the heads of seers. This describes a time of spiritual blindness or apostasy.

The whole vision has become like a sealed book. When it is given to a learned man to read, he says, “I can’t; it is sealed.” Latter-day Saints see fulfillment when Martin Harris showed characters from the gold plates to scholar Charles Anthon.

f.g: In Latter-day Saint understanding, Professor Charles Anthon of New York (1828).

n: Then the book is given to someone unlearned, who says, “I am not learned.” Joseph Smith, a farm boy with little schooling, translated the Book of Mormon by the gift and power of God.

The Lord explains why: the people honor Him with their lips but their hearts are far from Him, and their worship is based on human rules. Jesus quoted this; He also used similar words to Joseph Smith in the First Vision.

f.w: with their lips do honour me

n: So God will do “a marvellous work and a wonder,” confounding the wisdom of the wise. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the Restoration of the gospel and the coming forth of the Book of Mormon.

f.w: a marvellous work and a wonder
the wisdom of their wise men shall perish

n: Woe to those who try to hide their plans from the Lord, working in the dark and saying, “Who sees us?” Nephi applies this to secret combinations.
How twisted! They treat the Potter as if He were the clay. Can a thing say of its maker, “He didn’t make me” or “He doesn’t understand”?
In a very short time, Lebanon will become a fertile field and the fertile field a forest — a picture of dramatic transformation, including the renewal of the land.

f.w: Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field

n: In that day the deaf will hear the words of the book and the blind will see out of darkness. The Book of Mormon helps open spiritual eyes and ears.

f.w: the deaf hear the words of the book

n: The humble will find fresh joy in the Lord, and the poor will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.

f.w: The meek also shall increase their joy

n: The ruthless will disappear, mockers will be finished, and all who look for chances to do evil will be cut off.

f.g: Look for opportunities to do wrong.

n: These are people who make someone a criminal with a word, set traps for the one who defends justice at the city gate, and deny justice to the innocent with lies.

f.w: make a man an offender for a word

f.g: Speaks up for justice in court (held at the city gate).

n: The Lord, who redeemed Abraham, says Jacob will no longer be ashamed or turn pale with fear. Israel’s long disgrace will end.

f.g: Grow pale with fear or shame.

n: When Jacob sees his children — the work of God’s hands — gathered around him, they will honor God’s name and stand in awe of the Holy One of Jacob.

f.w: his children, the work of mine hands

n: Those who wandered in spirit will gain understanding, and complainers will accept instruction. Nephi links this to the Book of Mormon’s power to teach true doctrine.

f.w: they that murmured shall learn doctrine
